summary: Low-power wireless networks often need routes between two ordinary nodes, not just toward a central root. This document specifies AODV-RPL, which adapts the AODV route discovery approach to RPL so that peer-to-peer routes can be found for both symmetric and asymmetric links.

eli5.summary: Tiny sensors usually pass messages up to a boss. This lets one sensor ask around to find a direct path to another sensor, even if the path is better one way than the other.

subtitle: On-demand route discovery between two ordinary nodes in low-power wireless networks, even when links are better in one direction.

tldr.problem: In an RPL network, traffic between two ordinary routers usually has to travel via the root or a common ancestor, which makes routes longer and congests the area near the root. Links in low-power networks may also be better in one direction than the other.
tldr.mechanism: AODV-RPL borrows AODV's on-demand Route Request and Route Reply, carried as new options in RPL DIO messages. It builds a pair of RPL Instances, one for each direction, so each direction can use its own best path.
tldr.outcome: Peer-to-peer routes can be found when needed, as hop-by-hop or source routes, and symmetric or asymmetric. Some AODV features, such as route error flagging, are left out.

facts.value: 1/4 of the duration set by L

sections.title: Why Peer-to-Peer Routes in RPL
sections.content:
RPL is an IPv6 distance vector routing protocol that organizes a network as a root-based DODAG (Destination-Oriented Directed Acyclic Graph). Traffic between two routers inside the DODAG has to go through the root (in non-storing mode) or a common ancestor (in storing mode). Such peer-to-peer (P2P) traffic can take longer routes and cause congestion near the root.

AODV-RPL models route discovery on AODV (RFC 3561). Routes are found on demand, so they are only built when needed. The RFC says AODV-RPL currently omits some AODV features: flagging route errors, blocking the use of unidirectional links, multihoming and unnumbered interfaces.

It reuses RPL's DODAG formation, RPL Instances, Objective Functions, Trickle timers and storing and non-storing modes. It does not use the DAO control message. It uses the P2P Route Discovery Mode of Operation (MOP 4) with three new DIO options, and a new multicast group, so it does not conflict with P2P-RPL (RFC 6997).
sections.eli5: Normally two sensors talk by sending everything up to the boss and back down. AODV-RPL lets them find a shortcut directly between them, only when they need one.

sections.title: How Route Discovery Works
sections.content:
AODV-RPL is a reactive (on-demand) protocol. Discovery starts when the originating node (OrigNode) has data for a target node (TargNode) and has no route that satisfies the application's requirements. It works without needing RPL or any other routing protocol to be running.

The discovered routes are not forced through a common ancestor. The protocol builds paired DODAGs (two RPL Instances). The RREQ-Instance carries control messages from OrigNode to TargNode, and the route it finds is used for data from TargNode to OrigNode. The RREP-Instance carries control messages from TargNode to OrigNode, and its route is used for data from OrigNode to TargNode.

A route is symmetric when both directions traverse the same routers over the same links. It is asymmetric when the paths differ, for example because only one direction of some link satisfies the Objective Function. Intermediate routers join the DODAGs by Rank, as in RPL.
sections.eli5: To find a path, one sensor shouts a question outward, and the answer comes back along a path. Because the road may be better in one direction, the question road and the answer road can be different roads.

sections.title: The RREQ, RREP and ART Options
sections.content:
Three new DIO options carry the protocol. The RREQ option (type 0x0B) has flag bits S (symmetric route so far) and H (1 for hop-by-hop, 0 for source routing), a Compr field that elides address prefix octets in source routing, a 2-bit L lifetime for the temporary DAG, an 8-bit RankLimit, an Orig SeqNo, and an optional Address Vector listing the route so far. Exactly one RREQ option MUST be in an RREQ-DIO.

The RREP option (type 0x0C) has a G bit for gratuitous replies, the same H, Compr, L and RankLimit fields, and a 6-bit Delta that lets receivers match the reply to its request. The ART option (type 0x0D), short for AODV-RPL Target, is based on RPL's Target option. It holds the target's address or prefix and a Destination Sequence Number. An RREQ-DIO MUST carry at least one ART option and an RREP-DIO exactly one. Messages that break these rules MUST be dropped.

The L values are: 0x00 no time limit, 0x01 16 seconds, 0x02 64 seconds and 0x03 256 seconds. After the time is reached a node SHOULD leave the RREQ-Instance, and it MUST NOT rejoin for REJOIN_REENABLE, which defaults to 15 minutes.
sections.eli5: The messages have little checkboxes and numbers on them: how far to look, how long to keep asking, and who we are looking for. A message that is filled in wrong gets thrown away.

sections.title: Sending Requests and Replies
sections.content:
To start, OrigNode builds a local RPL Instance and a DODAG rooted at itself. It sends a DIO with exactly one RREQ option and at least one ART option to the multicast group all-AODV-RPL-nodes, with S=1 and an increased sequence number. Transmission follows the Trickle timer. One request may list several targets, but they must share the same Objective Function.

A router that receives an RREQ-DIO checks that it is valid and that it has resources, then asks whether the incoming link gives a usable route back to OrigNode under the Objective Function. If not, it drops the message. If so, it joins the RREQ-Instance with the sender as its preferred parent. With H=0 it drops the message if its own address is already in the Address Vector, and when it forwards it appends its address. It sets S=1 on the forwarded message only if the incoming S was 1 and the downward direction of the link also satisfies the Objective Function.

When the request reaches TargNode, it may wait RREP_WAIT_TIME, by default a quarter of the duration set by L, to see whether a better route arrives. For a symmetric route (S=1), the RREP-DIO is unicast back along the same route. For an asymmetric route (S=0), TargNode MUST build a DODAG in the RREP-Instance rooted at itself and multicast the RREP-DIO. Each router along the way joins if the downward direction of the link satisfies the Objective Function, and OrigNode starts sending data once it gets the reply.

Because RPLInstanceIDs are assigned locally, the two instances are paired. If TargNode finds the candidate ID already in use, it adds Delta to the request's ID, rolling over past 255 back to 0, so the pairing is preserved.
sections.eli5: One sensor yells "who can reach Sensor T?" and every helper repeats it only if it has a good road back. When T hears it, T sends the answer back, along the same road if it was good both ways, or by shouting again if the road home is different.

sections.title: Gratuitous Replies and Trickle
sections.content:
An intermediate router MAY unicast a Gratuitous RREP (G-RREP, G=1) back to OrigNode before passing the request on. It may do this when it already has a pair of downward and upward routes to the target that satisfy the Objective Function and whose Destination Sequence Number is at least as large as the one in the request. This lets OrigNode start sending sooner. The router then unicasts the RREQ toward TargNode, so the target also learns the route and the RREQ-InstanceID. An upstream router that receives a G-RREP MUST generate its own and send it further toward OrigNode.

Multicast RREQ-DIO and RREP-DIO transmissions are controlled by the Trickle timer (RFC 6206), following the DIO transmission procedure in RFC 6550. If the route is symmetric, the RREP-DIO does not need Trickle.
sections.eli5: A helper who already knows the way can call back right away and say "I know a route, start walking!" while it also passes the question along.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The risks are similar to those of RPL, and AODV-RPL relies on RPL's optional security framework for confidentiality, authentication, replay protection and delay protection. A router can join a secure route discovery only if it supports the security configuration in use and has the key.

A rogue router that knows the key could advertise false information, create bogus RREQ-DIO or RREP-DIO messages, alter genuine replies, or act as OrigNode to launch denial-of-service attacks with fake discoveries. When rogue routers might be present, RPL's preinstalled mode, where the key is preinstalled, SHOULD be used. A rogue router could also fill the Address Vector of a source-routed request so the reply loops, or forge a G-RREP to mount denial-of-service attacks.
sections.eli5: If a bad sensor knows the secret password, it can lie about roads or keep asking for useless directions to tire everyone out. Handing out the password ahead of time helps keep strangers out.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
AODV-RPL uses the P2P Route Discovery Mode of Operation (MOP 4), and this document was added as a reference for it. IANA assigned the three options in the RPL Control Message Options registry: 0x0B for RREQ, 0x0C for RREP and 0x0D for ART.

IANA also allocated the permanent link-local multicast address 224.0.0.69 for all-AODV-RPL-nodes in the IPv4 Multicast Address Space Registry.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers was updated so that these three message parts and the group shout-address have their own reserved numbers.

items.title: RREQ-Instance
items.text: Control messages go OrigNode to TargNode; the route it finds carries data from TargNode to OrigNode.

items.title: RREP-Instance
items.text: Control messages go TargNode to OrigNode; the route it finds carries data from OrigNode to TargNode.

items.title: Symmetric route
items.text: Both directions use the same routers over the same links (S=1).

items.title: Asymmetric route
items.text: At least one hop does not satisfy the Objective Function (S=0), so the two directions differ.

items.label: RREQ
items.desc: Route Request option, one per RREQ-DIO.

items.label: RREP
items.desc: Route Reply option, one per RREP-DIO.

items.label: ART
items.desc: AODV-RPL Target option naming the target or the originator.

items.label: 16 seconds
items.desc: Node leaves the RREQ-Instance after 16 seconds.
